stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

How to Build a Software Factory with Claude Code: From Vibe Coding to Agentic Development

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: Qwen Releases New Open-Weight Models: 3.8 Max (2.4T) and 27B, Aimed at Coding and 'Cowork'
stories.summary: Latent Space's AI News roundup reports that Qwen has released two new open-weight models — a large '3.8 Max' model cited at 2.4 trillion parameters, and a smaller 27B variant — positioned for coding and collaborative 'cowork' use cases. Both are being released as open weights, continuing Qwen's rapid cadence of model drops. Details beyond the roundup mention are limited.
stories.whyItMatters: Another large open-weight release from Qwen keeps pressure on Western labs' pricing and open-model strategy, especially for coding-focused use cases.
whatToWatch: Independent benchmarks comparing 3.8 Max and 27B against other open coding models
Licensing terms for commercial use
Uptake by inference providers and coding tool integrations
questions: Is the 2.4T parameter figure a total or active/MoE parameter count?
How does the 27B model perform relative to similarly-sized open models?

sources.title: [AINews] Qwen 3.8 Max(2.4T) and 27B, new open weights models for Coding and Cowork

stories.title: Essay Argues 'LLMs Reward Expertise'
stories.summary: A widely-discussed blog post argues that large language models reward users who already bring domain expertise to their prompts and evaluation, rather than leveling the playing field for novices. The piece, circulating on Hacker News, feeds an ongoing debate about who actually benefits most from AI coding and knowledge tools.
stories.whyItMatters: The claim cuts against a common narrative that AI tools democratize expertise, which matters for how enterprises think about training and hiring around AI adoption.
whatToWatch: Whether the argument gains traction among AI practitioners and educators
Any follow-up responses or counterarguments
questions: Does the effect hold across different LLMs and task types?

stories.title: Latent Space Hosts 'Inference Engineering Masterclass' with Baseten's Philip Kiely and Ali Taha
stories.summary: The Latent Space podcast published an episode billed as an 'Inference Engineering Masterclass,' featuring Baseten's Philip Kiely and Ali Taha discussing how to run model inference at scale. It adds to Latent Space's ongoing series of technical conversations with practitioners building AI infrastructure.
stories.whyItMatters: Inference cost and latency remain a central bottleneck for AI product economics, so practitioner-level detail from an infra vendor like Baseten is useful for teams making build-vs-buy decisions.
whatToWatch: Any specific techniques or benchmarks discussed that get picked up elsewhere
questions: What specific optimizations or tradeoffs does the episode highlight?

sources.title: The Inference Engineering Masterclass — Philip Kiely & Ali Taha, Baseten

stories.title: MiniMax H3 Gets Day-0 Support in ComfyUI, Bringing Open-Weight Native Audio and 2K Video
stories.summary: ComfyUI announced day-zero support for MiniMax's H3 model, which is being released with open weights and includes native audio generation alongside 2K video output. The integration lets ComfyUI users run the model immediately upon release rather than waiting for community ports.
stories.whyItMatters: Open-weight video/audio generation models with day-0 tooling support lower the barrier for developers and studios to experiment with multimodal generation without relying on closed APIs.
whatToWatch: Community benchmarks of H3's video and audio quality versus closed competitors
Licensing terms for commercial use of the open weights
questions: How does H3's 2K video quality and generation speed compare to leading closed models?

sources.title: MiniMax H3 Day-0 Support in ComfyUI: Open Weights, Native Audio, and 2K Video

stories.title: Researchers Question Whether Recent 'Critical' SQLite CVEs Are Real Bugs or LLM-Generated Slop
stories.summary: A JFrog research post examines a batch of recently filed 'critical' CVEs against SQLite and raises doubts about whether they represent genuine vulnerabilities or are low-quality reports produced with the help of LLMs. It's part of a broader pattern of security researchers flagging AI-assisted vulnerability submissions that don't hold up to scrutiny.
stories.whyItMatters: As AI tools make it trivially easy to generate plausible-looking but unsubstantiated vulnerability reports, this adds friction and noise to open-source security triage — a real cost of AI adoption in the security ecosystem.
whatToWatch: Whether SQLite maintainers formally respond to or dispute the flagged CVEs
Whether CVE assignment bodies tighten review standards in response
questions: How many of the disputed CVEs get retracted or downgraded?

sources.title: SQLite Critical CVEs or LLM Slop?

stories.title: OpenAI Details How It Built a Realtime Voice AI System in Six Months
stories.summary: OpenAI published an engineering blog post describing how its team built a realtime, responsive voice AI system over a six-month period. The post walks through the technical journey behind delivering low-latency conversational voice interactions.
stories.whyItMatters: Realtime voice is a key battleground for consumer and enterprise AI assistants, and engineering detail from OpenAI signals where the state of the art is heading on latency and responsiveness.
whatToWatch: Whether the techniques described get incorporated into OpenAI's public API or products
Competitor responses on voice latency benchmarks
questions: Which specific product(s) does this realtime system power?

sources.title: How we built a realtime system for responsive voice AI in six months

stories.title: Cloudflare Details Running Kimi and GLM Models at Scale: 'Smaller, Faster, Safer'
stories.summary: Cloudflare published a blog post describing its work running the Kimi and GLM open-weight model families at scale on its infrastructure, framed around making them smaller, faster, and safer to deploy. The post reflects the growing role of cloud/edge providers in serving Chinese open-weight models to a global developer base.
stories.whyItMatters: Major infrastructure providers hosting Kimi and GLM signals that these open models are becoming standard options in the mainstream inference stack, not just niche alternatives.
whatToWatch: Pricing and performance details Cloudflare shares for these models
Whether other major cloud providers follow with similar hosting offers
questions: What specific optimizations does Cloudflare apply to make these models 'smaller, faster, safer'?

sources.title: Smaller, faster, safer: running Kimi and GLM at scale

stories.title: Blog Post Argues Developers Should Manually Retype LLM-Generated Code to Avoid 'Cognitive Debt'
stories.summary: A blog post circulating on Hacker News argues that developers should manually retype AI-generated code rather than copy-pasting it, to avoid what the author calls 'cognitive debt' — a loss of understanding and skill from over-relying on AI output. It adds to an ongoing conversation about how AI coding tools affect developer learning and code comprehension.
stories.whyItMatters: As AI coding assistants become standard in software teams, how organizations manage the tradeoff between speed and engineer skill retention is a live and unresolved question.
whatToWatch: Whether the practice gets adopted or discussed further in engineering team norms
questions: Is there evidence beyond anecdote that manual retyping improves retention or code quality?

sources.title: Prevent cognitive debt by manually retyping LLM-generated code

stories.title: Show HN: A Version of Hacker News with AI Stories Filtered Out
stories.summary: A developer built and shared a tool that presents the Hacker News front page with AI-related stories filtered out, posted as a 'Show HN' submission. The project is a small, community-built response to the volume of AI content now dominating tech discussion forums.
stories.whyItMatters: The existence of a tool built specifically to avoid AI news is itself a data point on how saturated tech discourse has become with AI coverage.
whatToWatch: Whether the tool gains meaningful adoption or spawns similar filters elsewhere

stories.summary: Hoplite, a startup from Y Combinator's S26 batch, launched on Hacker News with a tool for deploying cloud-based coding agents. The Launch HN post is the company's public introduction of its product to the developer community.
stories.whyItMatters: The launch is another sign of how crowded the cloud coding-agent space has become, with new entrants continuing to target developer workflows around autonomous coding.

How Hoplite differentiates from other cloud coding-agent platforms

stories.title: Hacker News' Monthly 'Who Wants to Be Hired' Thread Returns for August 2026
stories.summary: Hacker News published its recurring monthly 'Who wants to be hired?' community thread for August 2026, where users post their skills and availability. It's not AI-specific, but these threads offer a rough, informal pulse-check on tech hiring sentiment, including for AI-related roles.
stories.whyItMatters: Recurring hiring threads offer an informal, low-cost signal of how tech workers — including those with AI skills — are positioning themselves in a shifting job market.
questions: Does this month's thread show any notable shift in AI-specific skills being advertised?
